title: The Sower and the Alphabet: Grasset from the Lausanne Workshop to the Cemetery at Sceaux
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Lausanne, the birth in the woodcarver's house
stops.date_confidence: attested; the house itself is not identified in any reachable source, and the pin marks the historic city centre
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of May a son is born to a Lausanne cabinetmaker and sculptor, and the boy learns the grain of walnut before he learns the alphabet. The father's shop is the first school: chisels, veneers, the discipline of an ornament that has to fit the object it covers. Vaud is a canton with no court and no academy, and its craftsmen work for churches, notaries and the lake trade. Nothing in the house suggests Paris. The argument he will make for the next sixty years is already lying on the bench in front of him: decoration is a trade before it is an art.
suggested_refs: The artisan quarters of Lausanne in the 1840s, cabinetmaking and church sculpture

stops.name: Lausanne, the lessons of François Bocion
stops.date_confidence: attested as a period, c. 1859-1863; no start or end date is documented and the month is a default
stops.campa: Through his teens he draws under François-Louis David Bocion, painter of the Lake Geneva shore, who teaches a generation of Vaudois boys to set a horizon and hold it. Bocion works in daylight on the water, in small canvases of barges and haze; his pupil takes from him not the subject but the primacy of the drawn line, laid down before any color arrives. The same teacher's roll carries Théophile Steinlen, who will also go to Paris and also live by the printed sheet, and who will also be known for cats and posters rather than for lakes.
suggested_refs: Bocion's lake paintings and his teaching practice in Lausanne

stops.name: Zurich, the Polytechnikum
stops.date_confidence: attested year of the move; matriculation record, term dates and reason for leaving are not in any reachable source, and the month is a default
stops.campa: He leaves the lake for Zurich and enrolls in architecture at the federal Polytechnicum. He does not finish. What he keeps is the habit of the section and the elevation: a building is a set of proportions before it is a surface, and ornament that ignores the structure under it is a lie told in paint. He will apply the rule to a stained-glass window, to a mosaic floor, to a page of type, and to the letters of an alphabet drawn forty years later. He leaves Zurich without a diploma. What he takes instead is the drawing habit of an architect.
suggested_refs: The Eidgenossisches Polytechnikum in the 1860s, its architecture course under Gottfried Semper

stops.name: Cairo, the year in Egypt
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; no city, route, duration or companion is named anywhere reachable, so the Cairo pin is a convention and not a documented location
stops.campa: At twenty-one he travels to Egypt. No source names a city, a route or a companion, and Cairo stands here only as the usual door into the country. What comes back with him is a grammar: flat fields of color held inside a hard contour, figures set in profile and stacked rather than modeled, borders of reed and lotus repeating without shadow. French drawing of the period wants depth and modeling. He has seen an art that refuses both and loses nothing by it, and he will spend a career proving the same on paper.
suggested_refs: European artists' Egyptian journeys of the 1860s and the ornament they brought back

stops.name: Lausanne, the theatre painter
stops.date_confidence: attested c. 1869-1870; the month is a default and the pin marks the town theatre
stops.campa: Back in his own town he paints scenery and carves for the Lausanne theatre, work done fast, at scale, to be read from the back of a hall by gaslight. It is the exact training a poster requires and nobody yet calls it that: large flat masses, a silhouette that survives at distance, a color that carries across a room. He is twenty-four, employed and provincial. In two years he will be in Paris designing wallpaper, and the scene-painter's arithmetic will still be the arithmetic he uses.
suggested_refs: Scene painting practice in provincial Swiss theatres of the 1860s

stops.name: Lausanne, Viollet-le-Duc in the town
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the meeting rests on en.wikipedia alone, unsourced there, and the Wikidata teacher record for Grasset names Bocion, not Viollet-le-Duc
stops.campa: Eugène Viollet-le-Duc is in the region in these years, and the young decorator meets him. The restorer of Vézelay, of Carcassonne and of Notre-Dame is also the loudest voice in Europe for a single doctrine: ornament must declare the structure it sits on. Nothing survives of what passed between them. The doctrine passes anyway: build the pattern out of the thing it covers, take the model from the plant and the crystal rather than from a Renaissance pattern book. Thirty-five years later Grasset will teach that argument to students as his own method.
sources: Wikidata Q524154 P1066, which names Bocion and not Viollet-le-Duc
suggested_refs: Viollet-le-Duc's Entretiens sur l'architecture and his Swiss years

segments.name: Paris and the Trades of Ornament

stops.name: Paris, the arrival in the year of the Commune
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is a default and the pin is the canonical Paris anchor
stops.campa: He settles in Paris in the year the city eats itself: siege, capitulation, the Commune, the Semaine sanglante, whole quarters burned. A Swiss decorator arrives into that and finds work, because a burned city needs furniture, wallpaper, fabric, tapestry, ceramic and jewelry, and he can draw all of them. He will live in France the rest of his life and work nowhere else. He marries Euphrasie Charlotte Charrotton, born at Gibraltar in 1848; the record does not preserve the date of the wedding.
suggested_refs: The Paris decorative trades in the reconstruction after 1871

stops.name: Paris, rue Thévenot, the jewelers' apprentices
stops.date_confidence: attested from 1875; the street has been absorbed into the redrawn 2nd arrondissement and the coordinate is approximate
stops.campa: He takes a post at the school on the rue Thévenot, teaching drawing to apprentices of the jewelry trade. It is the first of a chain of teaching posts running, with gaps, to the last year of his life. The pupils are not artists and are not meant to become artists; they are boys who will set stones and chase metal, and what they need is the ability to construct an ornament that fits a bezel. Explaining the work turns out to be a separate craft from doing it, and it is the one he practises longest.
suggested_refs: Trade drawing schools of the Paris jewelry quarter in the 1870s

stops.name: Paris, rue Madame, the house of Charles Gillot
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is a default
stops.campa: The printer Charles Gillot commissions him to decorate and furnish a townhouse on the rue Madame: paneling, furniture, glass, the whole interior as one designed object. Gillot's own trade is photorelief, the process that turns a drawn line into a printing plate without an engraver's intervening hand. The two men fit together like a plate and its press. Everything Grasset publishes for the next twenty years will depend on a technique that reproduces flat color and hard contour exactly, and here he is decorating the room of the man who owns it.
suggested_refs: Charles Gillot's gillotage process and his collection of Japanese art

stops.name: Paris, the office of Paris illustré
stops.date_confidence: attested from 1883; the magazine's address is not given in any reachable source and the pin marks central Paris
stops.campa: He begins drawing for the weekly Paris illustré, and the centre of his working life shifts from the room to the page. Applied decoration pays by the commission and dies with the house that holds it; a magazine goes out by the thousand and comes back as reputation. He is thirty-eight. From this year he makes his living by images that go through a press, and the furniture, the wallpaper and the tapestry drop back to occasional work he takes when it is offered.
suggested_refs: Paris illustré and the illustrated weeklies of the early 1880s

stops.name: Paris, the Four Sons of Aymon
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1883 by the works list; the month is a default chosen to order it after the magazine work of the same year
stops.campa: He illustrates the Histoire des Quatre Fils Aymon, the old chanson de geste of Renaud de Montauban and the horse Bayard, printed by Gillot in photorelief color. The book is medieval in subject and entirely modern in manufacture: flat inked areas, a heavy outline, ornament running into the text block instead of framing it politely at the margin. What is later called Art Nouveau on a poster hoarding is visible here first, inside the covers of a knightly romance, years before the hoardings fill up with it.
suggested_refs: Histoire des Quatre Fils Aymon (Paris: Launette, 1883), printed by Charles Gillot

stops.name: Paris, the workshop of Félix Gaudin
stops.date_confidence: attested from 1887; the collaboration runs to the end of his life and the month is a default
stops.campa: He begins working with the master glassmaker Félix Gaudin, who will realize his cartoons in lead and pot metal for thirty years and whom he will name executor of his will. Glass forces on a designer exactly what he already believes: every color is a bounded field, every field has a lead line around it, and no modeling is possible. The medium is the argument. Grasset works from the same conviction on paper, where nothing forces it on him, and the results look like windows.
suggested_refs: Félix Gaudin's atelier and the revival of French stained glass after 1880

segments.name: The Sower, the Chair, the Poster

stops.name: Paris, rue du Montparnasse, the sower of Larousse
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1890; the month is a default and the coordinate is approximate to the Librairie Larousse premises
stops.campa: For the Librairie Larousse he redraws the house mark: a nymph blowing the seeds off a dandelion clock, with the motto je sème à tout vent. The idea is Georges Moreau's, the publisher's co-founder, and the earlier logotype has been in use since 1876; what Grasset does is add the figure and give the whole thing its line. The popular account gives him the whole invention anyway. The mark outlives every poster he draws, printed on dictionaries sold in every French-speaking country for more than a century.
suggested_refs: The Larousse semeuse, from the 1876 mark to Grasset's 1890 redrawing

stops.name: Paris, rue Vavin, the chair of decorative composition
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1890 by en.wikipedia and to 1890/1891 elsewhere, held until 1903; the one-year spread is left open and the month is a default
stops.campa: He takes the chair of decorative composition at the École Guérin in Montparnasse and holds it thirteen years. He teaches the plant first: a stem is a structure, a leaf is a geometry, and the ornament is what remains after the botany is simplified rather than prettified. Among the students who pass through the room is Paul Berthon, who takes the method whole, keeps the flattened color and the vegetable line, and works it into lithographs so close to his teacher's hand that dealers still confuse the two.
stops.quote: La faculté de composition de l'ornement est donc un don poétique, comme il en faut un pour tous les autres arts, car ce don procède aussi de la vision préalable sans laquelle il ne peut exister que de pénibles arrangements dont les soudures et les disproportions montrent le côté artificiel.
stops.quote_source: Eugène Grasset, Méthode de composition ornementale, vol. I (1905), Introduction
suggested_refs: The École Guérin (École normale d'enseignement du dessin), rue Vavin and rue Bréa

stops.name: Paris, the Cité fleurie on the boulevard Arago
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1890s as a decade; no year is given for taking or leaving the studio, and both month and year here are placeholders inside that decade
stops.campa: His studio is in the Cité fleurie, a row of glass-roofed ateliers off the boulevard Arago, built out of salvaged pavilions from the Exposition Universelle of 1878. The rent is low, the light comes from the north, and the neighbors are painters and sculptors renting the same cheap sheds. Most of the poster and book work of the decade is drawn here, inside a building made from a demolished world's fair, by a man whose own designs will be shown at the next one.
suggested_refs: The Cité fleurie, 65 boulevard Arago, and its salvaged 1878 pavilions

stops.name: Paris, the decree of naturalization
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of June he becomes French, twenty years after arriving and at forty-six years of age. He has been a citizen of Vaud the whole time he has been furnishing, illustrating and teaching in Paris. The decree changes nothing in his practice and a good deal in the record: the state that will decorate him four years from now can do it as to one of its own, and the Swiss cabinetmaker's son enters French art history as a French designer.
suggested_refs: French naturalization decrees of 1891 and the Swiss colony in Paris

stops.name: Paris, the ink, the chocolate and the Place Clichy
stops.date_confidence: A la Place Clichy is dated 1891 and the Marquet and Masson posters 1892 by the works list; an earlier pass dated the Marquet sheet 1895, which the same list contradicts
stops.campa: In two years he draws a department store, a chocolate maker and an ink. Encre L. Marquet, la meilleure de toutes les encres: a woman in profile at a writing desk, the bottle set on the sheet like a liturgical object, the whole built of outline and flat ground. A poster is an advertisement for eight days and a print for a hundred years, and collectors are already buying them off the hoardings before the paste dries. The Rijksmuseum holds the Marquet sheet now, in a case, in another country.
stops.quote: Il est comme une manière de manifester notre plaisir de vivre et part d'une disposition plutôt heureuse de l'esprit ainsi que s'il s'agissait des apprêts d'une fête.
stops.quote_source: Eugène Grasset, Méthode de composition ornementale, vol. I (1905), Introduction, on ornament
sources: Wikidata SPARQL over P170 and P195, returning the Rijksmuseum
suggested_refs: Encre L. Marquet (1892), Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam

stops.name: New York, the Christmas Harper's
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Christmas number of 1892; the pin marks Harper & Brothers at Franklin Square, the client, since no source places Grasset in the United States
stops.campa: Harper's Magazine, published from Franklin Square in Manhattan, puts a Grasset drawing on its Christmas number. He does not travel; the drawing does. American readers meet the flat contour and the vegetable border on a newsstand two years before anyone in New York is using the words Art Nouveau, and American designers begin copying a Paris manner out of a magazine cover. No source consulted places him in the United States at any point in his life.
suggested_refs: Harper's Magazine Christmas number, 1892, and the American poster craze that followed

stops.name: London, the Grafton Galleries
stops.date_confidence: 1893 per en.wikipedia; an earlier pass reported a spread of 1892, 1893 and 1894 that could not be reproduced in either article, and the month is a default
stops.campa: French decorative artists are shown at the Grafton Galleries in Mayfair, Grasset among them. London is where the argument he works from was first made loudly: that a wallpaper and a cathedral window are one discipline, and that ornament without structure is a moral failure as well as an ugly one. He arrives as a Frenchman by decree and a Swiss by birth, showing the doctrine back to the country that exported it, in a season when English buyers are learning to collect French lithographs.
suggested_refs: The Grafton Galleries exhibitions of French decorative art, early 1890s

stops.name: New York, the Century Magazine
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1894; the pin marks The Century Co. at 33 East 17th Street on Union Square, the client, not the artist, and the month is a default
stops.campa: The Century Magazine, published from East Seventeenth Street on Union Square, prints The Wooly Horse and The Sun of Austerlitz to his design. It is the second American house to buy from him in three years, and again the work crosses the ocean without him. One subject is a frontier hoax and the other is Napoleon's sunrise at Austerlitz, both drawn in Montparnasse by a man who has seen neither. New York's own poster boom begins the same year, on paper that looks like this.
suggested_refs: The Century Magazine, 1894, and the New York poster boom of 1894-1896

stops.name: Paris, the Salon des Cent
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1894; the day is a default
stops.campa: His prints and posters hang at the Salon des Cent, the exhibition run by the magazine La Plume out of its rooms on the rue Bonaparte, where the entrance costs almost nothing and the sheets on the wall are for sale at prices a clerk can meet. The Salon is where the poster stops being commercial waste and becomes something collected, catalogued and framed. A Paris buyer who knows the trade can name him from the drawing alone, without looking in the corner for a signature.
suggested_refs: The Salon des Cent and the La Plume rooms, 31 rue Bonaparte

stops.name: Paris, the Maid for Sarah Bernhardt
stops.date_confidence: the works list dates the Jeanne d'Arc poster to 1894 in two versions; an earlier pass gave 1889-1890 and a different theatre, which that house's own chronology contradicts, and the month is a default
stops.campa: He draws Jeanne d'Arc for Sarah Bernhardt: the Maid in white armor against a field of fleurs-de-lis, haloed, in profile, holding the standard, the whole sheet built like a window in a church, with the outlines standing in for lead. There are two versions. It is reproduced more than anything else he draws, and it is what the public takes his manner to be: a religious composition sold as a theatre bill, pasted up on hoardings beside advertisements for bicycles and cigarette paper.
suggested_refs: Grasset's Jeanne d'Arc lithograph for Sarah Bernhardt, two versions

stops.name: Paris, Chevalier of the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Wikidata award qualifier and corroborated in the French biography
stops.campa: On the seventh of May the Republic makes him a chevalier of the Legion of Honour, four years after granting him its nationality. Frantz Jourdain profiles him in Les Décorés, and the critical language of the year lists him among the painters of the Salon rather than among tradesmen, without apology and without explanation. The poster and the ceiling are being written about as one art by critics who used to separate them, and the state, late as usual, has just agreed.
suggested_refs: Frantz Jourdain, Les Décorés, on Grasset

stops.name: Troyes, the life of Saint Joseph
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1894 by the works list; the month is a default
stops.campa: At the church of the Madeleine in Troyes he sets a life of Saint Joseph into glass and mosaic, executed with Gaudin. Champagne is the old capital of French stained glass and the town keeps sixteenth-century windows in most of its churches; he works beside them without imitating them. The figures are his own, flat, outlined, unmodeled, the drapery falling in patterns rather than folds. What the medieval glaziers did because lead required it, he does because he has decided it is right.
suggested_refs: Église de la Madeleine, Troyes, and the sixteenth-century glass of Champagne

stops.name: Briare, the enamel floor of Saint-Étienne
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1894-1895; the month is a default and the coordinate corrects an earlier pin about a kilometre north-east of the church
stops.campa: The little town of Briare on the Loire makes buttons and enamel tesserae in the Bapterosses works, and its new church, built between 1890 and 1895, is paved with them to Grasset's designs, the windows realized by Gaudin. Beasts, birds and interlace run across the floor in colored enamel, an ornament walked on rather than looked up at. It is the least perishable thing he ever makes: paper yellows, posters are pasted over within the month, and a mosaic floor in a parish church stays where it is put.
suggested_refs: The Manufacture des émaux de Briare and the floors of Saint-Étienne de Briare

stops.name: Paris, La Plante et ses applications ornementales
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1896 by the works list; the month is a default
stops.campa: He publishes La Plante et ses applications ornementales, plate after plate in which a species is drawn from life, then reduced, then geometrized, then repeated into a border, a tile, a fabric, a grille. It is a method book and not a pattern book: the student is not handed ornaments to copy but the operation that produces them. Iris, thistle, hazel, dandelion. The argument, which is Viollet-le-Duc's argument taught to draughtsmen, is that nature supplies the structure and the designer supplies only the simplification.
stops.quote: L'ornement est né du désir d'exercer notre fantaisie en dehors de l'imitation pure et simple des objets naturels.
stops.quote_source: Eugène Grasset, Méthode de composition ornementale, vol. I (1905), Introduction
suggested_refs: La Plante et ses applications ornementales (Paris, 1896), plates by Grasset and his students

stops.name: Paris, the lecture called L'Art nouveau
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the source names the Union centrale des arts décoratifs and not a room, and the pin is a central-Paris approximation, since the body did not occupy the Pavillon de Marsan until 1905
stops.campa: On the eleventh of April he stands before the Union centrale des arts décoratifs and delivers a lecture titled L'Art nouveau. It is one of the few occasions on which he states the method in words instead of demonstrating it in plates: a decorative art built out of structure and out of observed nature, not out of the copying of historical styles. The term is barely two years old in Paris and already contested. He uses it as a program rather than a label, and keeps his distance from the whiplash line it is coming to mean.
stops.quote: ...c'est la façon personnelle d'exprimer des idées connues qui constitue le talent et l'originalité.
stops.quote_source: Eugène Grasset, Méthode de composition ornementale, vol. I (1905), Introduction, sidenote Innovation
suggested_refs: The Union centrale des arts décoratifs lecture series of 1897

stops.name: Paris, the seven volumes of the Nouveau Larousse
stops.date_confidence: attested as running 1897 to 1904; the month is a default and the reported Petit Larousse work of 1905 rests on a works list that names no plates
stops.campa: For seven years he illustrates the Nouveau Larousse illustré, seven volumes of a dictionary that intends to picture everything: tools, fish, uniforms, engines, the parts of a flower. It is the opposite pole of his practice from the poster. A poster has one image and eight days; an encyclopedia has ten thousand images and expects to be consulted for fifty years. The same hand does both, and one rule governs both, that the drawing must state what the thing is before it states anything else.
suggested_refs: Nouveau Larousse illustré, 7 vols. (1897-1904)

stops.name: Paris, the patent of the seventh of October
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by en.wikipedia; the foundry's address in this period is not confirmed and the pin marks central Paris
stops.campa: The typeface is patented. He has drawn a complete roman alphabet: narrow, slightly angular, the terminals cut rather than blunted, a face meant to carry the new decoration into ordinary text rather than to shout from a hoarding. A designer of wallpapers and church floors has arrived at the smallest and most disciplined unit of the trade, the letter, which must be legible at eight points and repeated a million times without anybody noticing who drew it.
stops.quote: La composition de cet ornement abstrait est la clef de toute autre composition artistique, quelle qu'elle puisse être.
stops.quote_source: Eugène Grasset, Méthode de composition ornementale, vol. I (1905), Principes généraux
suggested_refs: The Grasset typeface patent of 7 October 1897

stops.name: Paris, Peignot cuts the letters
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1898 for the foundry's issue, with the drawing and patent belonging to 1897; one summary source dates the design itself to 1898, conflicting with both articles, and the month is a default
stops.campa: G. Peignot et Fils cuts and casts the face and sells it simply as Grasset. A foundry is a slow machine: punches cut by hand, matrices struck, metal cast in sizes, specimens printed and mailed to every jobbing printer in France. The alphabet passes out of the designer's hands and into the cases of men he will never meet, who will set it into wine labels, timetables and municipal notices. It is the widest distribution any of his drawing achieves, and none of it carries an image.
stops.quote: L'ornement primitif ou abstrait est composé presque uniquement des éléments géométriques simples, ceux que chacun connaît sans avoir nécessairement fait de la géométrie une étude spéciale.
stops.quote_source: Eugène Grasset, Méthode de composition ornementale, vol. I (1905), Principes généraux
suggested_refs: Fonderie G. Peignot et Fils specimen books showing the Grasset face

stops.name: Paris, the Champ de Mars
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1900 Exposition Universelle; the day given is the fair's opening rather than a documented date for his exhibit
stops.campa: At the Exposition Universelle his type is shown to the public and his tapestry Fête de printemps is exhibited. Fifty million visitors come through the fairground in seven months. The decorative art of France is assembled in one season on one field, and the Swiss theatre painter's work stands in it as a matter of course, metal type in a case and a tapestry on a wall. No later year puts his name in front of so many people. The poster decade is ending, and nobody announces it.
suggested_refs: The 1900 Exposition Universelle decorative art displays on the Champ de Mars

stops.name: Sceaux, the house the Curies left
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1900; the house is not further identified, no lease or address survives, and the month is a default
stops.campa: He leaves Paris for Sceaux, a town of gardens south of the city, and takes a house the family of Eugène Curie has lived in; the street will be renamed for Pierre Curie in 1907. He is fifty-five. From here he commutes in to his classrooms and out to his printers with finished work under his arm, and he will not move again. Paul Berthon, who learned the method from him on the rue Vavin, will end his own life in this same town in 1934. Neither house carries a plaque.
suggested_refs: The rue Pierre-Curie at Sceaux and the Curie family's house there

stops.name: Paris, the Type Grasset for Indochina
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1904 by the works list; the month is a default and the pin marks the design's origin, not its circulation
stops.campa: Postage stamps for French Indochina are issued in the type that bears his name. A drawing made in a Montparnasse studio is engraved, printed, gummed, and licked onto letters in Saigon, Hanoi and Phnom Penh, and travels further than the man ever does. He has been to Egypt once and to London perhaps once; his letters go around the world in a colonial mailbag. It is the last new use his lettering is put to in his lifetime, and the smallest: a face drawn for books, reduced to the size of a thumbnail and sold across a post office counter.
suggested_refs: The Type Grasset postage issues of French Indochina, 1904

stops.name: Paris, rue Madame, the École d'art graphique
stops.date_confidence: attested c. 1903-1904; the dates are given loosely in the source and the month is a default
stops.campa: The thirteen years at the École Guérin end and he takes a short post at the École d'art graphique on the rue Madame, the same street where he furnished Gillot's house twenty-three years earlier. He is fifty-eight and has taught almost without interruption since 1875. The commissions are thinning; Art Nouveau is beginning to be spoken of in the past tense by the men who invented the phrase. The classroom is now the principal place where his work is done.
suggested_refs: The École d'art graphique, rue Madame, in the 1900s

stops.name: Paris, the Académie de la Grande Chaumière
stops.date_confidence: attested as running 1904 to 1913; the month is a default
stops.campa: For nine years he teaches at the Académie de la Grande Chaumière in Montparnasse, an open studio where a student pays by the week, works from the model, and takes criticism from whichever master is in the room. Painters and sculptors come through it from every country in Europe and beyond. He gives them the instruction he gave the jewelers' apprentices on the rue Thévenot thirty years earlier: find the structure, simplify it, and decorate nothing you have not first understood.
suggested_refs: The Académie de la Grande Chaumière, 14 rue de la Grande Chaumière

stops.name: Paris, the École Estienne
stops.date_confidence: the post is attested and runs to his death, but no source gives a start year; 1904 is inferred from the other teaching dates and the month is a default
stops.campa: At the school for the graphic trades on the boulevard Auguste-Blanqui he teaches the history of letters and drawing to boys who will spend their lives in printing houses. The face he drew is by now in the cases they will work from, so the curriculum includes his own alphabet, taught by the man whose hand drew every letter of it. The face is anonymous in use: the name belongs to the specimen book and the foundry catalogue, never to the printed page. He keeps the post until the year he dies, when the older boys in his classes are being called up.
suggested_refs: The École Estienne, 18 boulevard Auguste-Blanqui, and its lettering curriculum

stops.name: Paris, the Méthode de composition ornementale
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1905; the month is a default
stops.campa: The Librairie centrale des Beaux-Arts publishes the Méthode de composition ornementale in two volumes, the summary of everything he has taught since the rue Thévenot. It begins with straight lines and nothing else, builds the grid, the rosette and the interlace out of them, and only then admits the plant. It ends where a manual has to stop: the operation can be taught to anyone, and running it well takes a gift the book says plainly it cannot supply.
stops.quote: Le but de l'Art Ornemental est donc, comme son nom l'indique, d'orner les objets fabriqués qui, de nus qu'ils sont en construction pure, deviennent comme habillés pour le plaisir de l'œil.
stops.quote_source: Eugène Grasset, Méthode de composition ornementale, vol. I (1905), Principes généraux, p. 1
suggested_refs: Méthode de composition ornementale, 2 vols. (Paris: Librairie centrale des Beaux-Arts, 1905)

stops.name: Paris, Officier de la Légion d'honneur
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Wikidata award qualifier and corroborated in the French biography
stops.campa: On the twentieth of October he is promoted officier, sixteen years after the first cross. He is sixty-six, teaching in two schools, and no longer drawing posters; the men who once bought sheets off the hoardings are buying cinema bills. The honor arrives at the end of the work rather than in the middle of it, which is the ordinary timing of French honors, and it is given for a body of work no single word covers: furniture, glass, mosaic, wallpaper, encyclopedia plates, one alphabet.
stops.quote: Le vrai talent n'a guère de concurrence à redouter, et celui qui en est doué peut travailler au grand jour sans crainte d'être égalé.
stops.quote_source: Eugène Grasset, Méthode de composition ornementale, vol. I (1905), Introduction

stops.name: Sceaux, the twenty-third of October
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; all three records of the death agree on Sceaux, and an earlier report of dissent between them was an artifact of machine summary, not a reading of any source
stops.campa: He dies at Sceaux at seventy-two, in the rented house on the street newly named for Pierre Curie, in the fourth year of a war that has emptied his classrooms and halted the trade he lived by. The posters that made his name are a quarter of a century old and belong to a period the men in the trenches have no memory of at all. The alphabet, meanwhile, is still being set daily in printing houses across France, on labels and timetables, with no name on it but his.
suggested_refs: Death notices for Grasset in the Paris art press, autumn 1917

stops.name: Sceaux, the decennial concession
stops.date_confidence: the burial and the ten-year concession are attested to the day; the later reclamation around 1927 is given as probable by the source itself and is not documented
stops.campa: Three days later he is buried in the cemetery of Sceaux in a ten-year concession, the temporary grade of French grave, renewable and otherwise reclaimed. Nobody renews it. The French account holds it probable that the plot was taken back around 1927 and the remains moved to the common ossuary kept for expired concessions; it says probable and not certain, and no later record settles the question. Where the body of the man who drew the Larousse sower now lies is not known.
suggested_refs: Registers of the Cimetière de Sceaux and French rules on concessions décennales

stops.name: Paris, the Hôtel Drouot, four sales
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1918; the day is a default
stops.campa: Five months after the funeral his studio and his collection go under the hammer at the Hôtel Drouot in four separate sales: Japanese prints, Greek vases, Tanagra figurines, medieval antiquities, and the working contents of a fifty-year practice. Félix Gaudin, the glassmaker named executor in the will of 1904, oversees the dispersal. The collection that taught him flat color and hieratic profile leaves the room in lots, bought mostly by people who do not know whose eye assembled it.
suggested_refs: The four Grasset estate sales at the Hôtel Drouot, March 1918, and their catalogues

stops.name: Lausanne, the retrospective of 2011
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2011 by the exhibition catalogue citation; the month is a default
stops.campa: The Musée cantonal des Beaux-Arts in the town where he was born mounts Eugène Grasset: l'art et l'ornement, the first full retrospective in a century. The cabinetmaker's son comes home as a Swiss claim on a French career. His work is held in Paris and Amsterdam, in Ottawa and Melbourne, in Kansas City and New York; and the mark he drew for a dictionary in 1890 is still on the covers in the museum shop, blowing seeds off a dandelion clock into whatever wind is going.
suggested_refs: Catalogue: Eugène Grasset, l'art et l'ornement (Musée cantonal des Beaux-Arts, Lausanne, 2011)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a line in a catalogue
stops.date_confidence: not a journey and not a dated event: a museum record of uncertain standing, entered here at the nominal date of the pass that could neither confirm nor refute it
stops.campa: A structured record says the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes on the Avenida del Libertador holds a work of his, and cites the museum's own site for it. The museum's search returns nothing that confirms the line, and neither the French nor the English nor the Spanish account of his life mentions Argentina, an Argentine exhibition, or an Argentine buyer. The sheet, if it exists, crossed the Atlantic the way the Harper's cover did, without him. Nothing settles the matter either way.
sources: Negative finding: no Argentina reference in en, fr or es Wikipedia or in Grasset's own writings
